## Statement

Adopt the Schwarzschild vacuum exterior model with $m_*>0$, $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2>0$ and $f(r)=1-s/r$, together with its ideal-free-fall rule that a massive test body follows a future timelike geodesic. For a fixed angular-momentum magnitude $\ell>0$, set

$$W_\ell(r)=f(r)\left(c^2+\frac{\ell^2}{r^2}\right),\qquad r>s.$$

The equatorial reduced radial system is

$$\dot r=w,\qquad \dot w=-\frac12 W_\ell'(r),$$

where dot denotes proper-time derivative and $\ell$ is held fixed. For every circular timelike radius $r_c>3s/2$, the corresponding equilibrium is

$$z_c=(r_c,0),\qquad \ell^2=\frac{c^2s r_c^2}{2r_c-3s}.$$

Then this equilibrium is Lyapunov stable in the Euclidean phase space $(r,w)$ when $r_c>3s$, and is not Lyapunov stable when $3s/2<r_c\le3s$. At $r_c=3s$ the equilibrium is a stationary inflection of $W_\ell$, not a strict extremum, and is still not Lyapunov stable. These are conclusions about the reduced radial system at fixed $\ell$ only.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stated Schwarzschild vacuum model, its free-fall rule, $c,s>0$, a fixed $\ell>0$, and the reduced radial state space $(s,\infty)\times\mathbb R$.

[A1] The adopted Schwarzschild model uses the exterior datum and ideal freely falling massive test bodies follow future timelike geodesics; this is a model assumption, not an empirical premise ([[pthm-gr-schwarzschild-vacuum-model]], [[post-gr-ideal-clocks-and-free-fall]]).

[F1] For an equatorial timelike geodesic with fixed conserved angular momentum $\ell$, the radial equation is $\dot r^2=e^2-W_\ell(r)$ and, on a radial interval, $\ddot r=-W_\ell'(r)/2$ ([[lem-gr-schwarzschild-timelike-geodesic-reduction]]).

[F2] A circular timelike orbit at $r_c>3s/2$ has $\ell^2=c^2s r_c^2/(2r_c-3s)$; the published supplier defines $V_\ell=W_\ell/2$ and gives $V_\ell''(r_c)=c^2s(r_c-3s)/(r_c^3(2r_c-3s))$, so $W_\ell''(r_c)=2c^2s(r_c-3s)/(r_c^3(2r_c-3s))$ at fixed $\ell$. Its sign gives a strict local minimum for $r_c>3s$ and a strict local maximum for $3s/2<r_c<3s$ ([[lem-gr-schwarzschild-circular-orbits-and-photon-sphere]] clause (c)).

[F3] Lyapunov stability quantifies over every sufficiently small Euclidean initial-state ball and every maximal solution, requiring forward existence for all $t\ge0$ and continued containment in a prescribed ball ([[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]]).

[F4] The smooth radial vector field is locally Lipschitz, so every initial state has a unique local solution ([[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]).

[F5] A solution of an autonomous locally Lipschitz ODE whose state remains in a compact subset of its open state domain near a finite endpoint extends beyond that endpoint ([[thm-cm-compact-continuation-for-locally-lipschitz-odes]] clause 2).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** reduce geodesic motion to the fixed-$\ell$ radial ODE, use its conserved one-dimensional energy, and apply the definition of Lyapunov stability plus compact continuation.


1.1 By [F1], the reduced vector field is $F_\ell(r,w)=(w,-W_\ell'(r)/2)$ on the open set $(s,\infty)\times\mathbb R$. It is smooth there and [F4] gives a unique local solution through every state. Differentiating $W_\ell=f(c^2+\ell^2/r^2)$ gives $W_\ell'=c^2s/r^2-2\ell^2/r^3+3s\ell^2/r^4$; substituting the circular value of $\ell^2$ from [F2] yields $W_\ell'(r_c)=0$, so $F_\ell(r_c,0)=0$. Along every solution, $H_\ell(r,w):=\tfrac12(w^2+W_\ell(r))$ satisfies $dH_\ell/d\tau=w(-W_\ell'/2)+(W_\ell'/2)w=0$. Thus $H_\ell$ is constant on each solution interval. [given, F1, F2, F4, algebra]

2.1 Suppose $r_c>3s$. By [F2], $W_\ell''(r_c)>0$, so continuity gives an interval about $r_c$ on which $W_\ell''>0$. Since $W_\ell'(r_c)=0$, the derivative is negative to the left and positive to the right there; hence $W_\ell$ has a strict local minimum. Fix any phase-space radius $\varepsilon>0$ whose closed ball about $z_c$ lies in $(s,\infty)\times\mathbb R$. Choose $0<\eta<\varepsilon/2$ so $[r_c-\eta, r_c+\eta]\subset(s,\infty)$ and both boundary values of $W_\ell$ exceed $W_\ell(r_c)$. By continuity of $H_\ell$, choose $0<\delta\le\varepsilon$ so every state within $\delta$ of $z_c$ has $|r-r_c|<\eta/2$, energy below both boundary potential halves, and $H_\ell-W_\ell(r_c)/2<\varepsilon^2/8$. Conservation in 1.1 prevents such a solution from reaching either radial boundary, since there $H_\ell\ge W_\ell(r_c\pm\eta)/2$. Inside the resulting radial interval $W_\ell(r)\ge W_\ell(r_c)$, so $w^2/2=H_\ell-W_\ell(r)/2<\varepsilon^2/8$ and $|w|<\varepsilon/2$. The state stays in a compact subset of the open domain; [F5] rules out a finite forward maximal endpoint. With $|r-r_c|<\eta<\varepsilon/2$ and $|w|<\varepsilon/2$, it remains inside the prescribed phase-space ball for every $\tau\ge0$. This is Lyapunov stability by [F3]. [step 1.1, F2, F3, F4, F5, algebra, algebra]

2.2 Suppose $3s/2<r_c<3s$. By [F2], $W_\ell''(r_c)<0$; shrink $\eta>0$ so $W_\ell'(r)<0$ on $(r_c,r_c+\eta]$. For any proposed initial-state radius $\delta>0$, choose $r_0\in(r_c,r_c+\min\{\eta/2,\delta/2\})$ and initial data $(r_0,0)$. [F4] supplies a local solution. Its acceleration is $-W_\ell'(r_0)/2>0$, and conservation of $H_\ell$ gives, on the outgoing branch, $w=\sqrt{W_\ell(r_0)-W_\ell(r)}$. The solution reaches $r_c+\eta$ in finite time: the travel-time integral is $\int_{r_0}^{r_c+\eta}[W_\ell(r_0)-W_\ell(r)]^{-1/2}dr$, whose only endpoint singularity is bounded by a constant times $(r-r_0)^{-1/2}$ because $W_\ell'(r_0)<0$. Hence initial data arbitrarily close to $z_c$ leave the fixed neighborhood of radius $\eta$, contradicting [F3]. [step 1.1, F2, F3, F4, algebra, algebra]

2.3 At $r_c=3s$, the circular relation gives $\ell^2=3c^2s^2$. Differentiating $W_\ell(r)=c^2(1-s/r)+\ell^2(r^{-2}-sr^{-3})$ at this fixed $\ell$ gives $W_\ell'(r)=c^2s(r-3s)^2/r^4$ and $W_\ell''(r)=-2c^2s(r-3s)(r-6s)/r^5$. Thus $W_\ell'$ is positive except at $3s$ and $W_\ell''$ changes sign there, so the equilibrium is a stationary inflection. Fix $0<\eta<s$ and, for any $\delta>0$, choose $r_0\in(3s-\min\{\eta/2,\delta/2\},3s)$ with initial data $(r_0,0)$. [F4] supplies a local solution. The acceleration is negative. On the inward branch energy conservation yields $w=-\sqrt{W_\ell(r_0)-W_\ell(r)}$ for $3s-\eta\le r<r_0$, since $W_\ell$ is strictly increasing on that interval. The travel-time integral to $3s-\eta$ is finite; near $r_0$ its integrand is bounded by a constant times $(r_0-r)^{-1/2}$ because $W_\ell'(r_0)>0$. Thus arbitrarily close initial data leave the fixed neighborhood of radius $\eta$, so [F3] says the equilibrium is not Lyapunov stable. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra, algebra]

3.1 The two subcritical cases in 2.2–2.3 are not Lyapunov stable, while the supercritical case in 2.1 is Lyapunov stable. These are deductions under the adopted Schwarzschild free-fall model [A1] and concern only its fixed-angular-momentum radial subsystem. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, A1, given] ∎
## Remarks

- The endpoint $r_c=3s$ is degenerate: $W_\ell''(r_c)=0$. The one-sided energy argument above establishes instability without calling the potential maximum or minimum.
- The statement does not perturb $\ell$ and does not imply orbital stability in the full geodesic phase space.

## Example

Use $s>0$ and the reduced potential $W_\ell(r)=(1-s/r)(c^2+\ell^2/r^2)$ of [[pthm-rpm-schwarzschild-circular-stability]]. At a circular orbit, $\ell^2=c^2sr_0^2/(2r_0-3s)$.

1. **Stable radial equilibrium at $r_0=4s$.** The circular value is $\ell^2=16c^2s^2/5$, and

   $$W_\ell''(4s)=\frac{2c^2s(4s-3s)}{(4s)^3(8s-3s)}=\frac{c^2}{160s^2}>0.$$

   The fixed-$\ell$ radial equilibrium is Lyapunov stable.
2. **Unstable radial equilibrium at $r_0=2s$.** Here $\ell^2=4c^2s^2$ and

   $$W_\ell''(2s)=\frac{2c^2s(2s-3s)}{(2s)^3(4s-3s)}=-\frac{c^2}{4s^2}<0.$$

   The fixed-$\ell$ equilibrium is unstable.
3. **Degenerate endpoint at $r_0=3s$.** Here $\ell^2=3c^2s^2$ and $W_\ell'(r)=c^2s(r-3s)^2/r^4$. It has a stationary inflection rather than a strict extremum, and the radial equilibrium is not Lyapunov stable by the one-sided perturbation argument in the theorem.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $s,c>0$, the Schwarzschild radial potential, and the fixed-angular-momentum stability theorem.

[F1] At a timelike circular orbit $r_0>3s/2$, $\ell^2=c^2sr_0^2/(2r_0-3s)$ and $V_\ell''(r_0)=c^2s(r_0-3s)/(r_0^3(2r_0-3s))$ for $V_\ell=W_\ell/2$ ([[lem-gr-schwarzschild-circular-orbits-and-photon-sphere]] clause (c)).

[F2] For the fixed-$\ell$ radial system, radii $r_0>3s$ are Lyapunov stable and radii $3s/2<r_0\le3s$ are not ([[pthm-rpm-schwarzschild-circular-stability]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** substitute each radius in the exact circular angular-momentum and potential-curvature formulas, then apply the radial stability theorem.


1.1 At $r_0=4s$, substitution gives $\ell^2=c^2s(16s^2)/(8s-3s)=16c^2s^2/5$ and [F1] gives $W_\ell''=2V_\ell''=c^2/(160s^2)>0$. Since $4s>3s$, [F2] classifies the equilibrium as Lyapunov stable in the fixed-$\ell$ radial state. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 At $r_0=2s$, substitution gives $\ell^2=4c^2s^2$ and $W_\ell''=2V_\ell''=-c^2/(4s^2)<0$. Since $3s/2<2s<3s$, [F2] classifies this equilibrium as unstable. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 At $r_0=3s$, substitution gives $\ell^2=3c^2s^2$. The formula for $W_\ell'$ in [F1] at this angular momentum is $c^2s(r-3s)^2/r^4$, positive away from $3s$ and zero at $3s$. The equilibrium is a stationary inflection; [F2] classifies it as not Lyapunov stable. All three results are restricted radial-model classifications. [F1, F2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2>0$, $f(r)=1-s/r$, and let $r_E,r_R>s$ be the emitter and receiver radii of static observers in the adopted Schwarzschild exterior model. With $n=f^{-1/2}\partial_0$ the unit static congruence and $U=cn$ the corresponding four-velocity, the ideal-clock and geometric-optics predictions are

$$\frac{\Delta\tau_R}{\Delta\tau_E}=\frac{\omega_E}{\omega_R}=\sqrt{\frac{f(r_R)}{f(r_E)}},\qquad \frac{\omega_R}{\omega_E}=\sqrt{\frac{f(r_E)}{f(r_R)}}.$$

The proper four-acceleration magnitude required to remain static at radius $r>s$ is

$$a(r)=\sqrt{g(\nabla_UU,\nabla_UU)}=\frac{c^2s}{2r^2\sqrt{f(r)}}=\frac{G_Nm_*}{r^2\sqrt{1-s/r}}.$$

For any $0\le\rho<1$ and radii satisfying $0<s/r_E,s/r_R\le\rho$, define $x_i=s/r_i$ and write $\log:=L$ for the natural integral logarithm of [[def-integral-logarithm]]. The exact logarithmic ratio has the uniform expansion

$$\log\frac{\omega_R}{\omega_E}=\frac{s}{2}\left(\frac1{r_R}-\frac1{r_E}\right)+R,\qquad |R|\le\frac{x_E^2+x_R^2}{4(1-\rho)}.$$

These are conditional deductions of the idealized model; no measured redshift or acceleration is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Schwarzschild vacuum exterior model with $s>0$, static observers at $r_E,r_R>s$, an ideal-clock reading of proper time, and the geometric-optics interpretation of the observer-energy ratio.

[A1] Ideal massive test bodies follow the adopted free-fall rule and ideal clocks record proper time; treating the observer-energy ratio as a frequency ratio is the geometric-optics convention ([[pthm-gr-schwarzschild-vacuum-model]], [[post-gr-ideal-clocks-and-free-fall]]).

[F1] The static congruence is $n=f^{-1/2}\partial_0$, with $g(n,n)=-1$, $\Delta\tau=\sqrt{f(r)}\Delta t$, and $\nabla_n n=(s/(2r^2))\partial_r$ ([[lem-gr-schwarzschild-static-congruence-and-clock-rates]] clauses (a), (c), (e)).

[F2] For a specified future null geodesic between static observers, $\omega_R/\omega_E=\sqrt{f(r_E)/f(r_R)}$ under the geometric-optics interpretation ([[pthm-gr-schwarzschild-stationary-redshift]] clauses (b), (d)).

[F3] In the Schwarzschild exterior $g_{rr}=f^{-1}$, $f=1-s/r$, and $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ ([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]).

[F4] The natural logarithm is the integral logarithm $L(y)=\int_1^y dt/t$ for $y>0$, and a continuous integrand has its integral function as a primitive ([[def-integral-logarithm]], [[thm-ftc-first-part]]).

[F5] If two continuous real functions satisfy $g\le h$ on an interval, their integrals preserve that order ([[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** combine the exact static observer identities and redshift ratio, scale the acceleration from unit observer to four-velocity, and bound the logarithmic remainder by an integral inequality.


1.1 By [F1], $U=cn$ is the static observer four-velocity because $g(U,U)=-c^2$. Since $c$ is constant, $\nabla_UU=c^2\nabla_nn=c^2s\partial_r/(2r^2)$. With $g(\partial_r,\partial_r)=f^{-1}$ from [F3], its squared norm is $c^4s^2/(4r^4f)$, so its positive magnitude is $c^2s/(2r^2\sqrt f)$. Substituting $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ gives the displayed Newton-constant form. [F1, F3, algebra]

1.2 Over the same coordinate-time interval, [F1] gives $\Delta\tau_R/\Delta\tau_E=\sqrt{f(r_R)/f(r_E)}$. [F2] gives the inverse ratio for received to emitted ideal-ray frequency, so the two displayed exact ratios follow. Each ratio is a conditional model result for the specified static observers and ideal ray. [A1, F1, F2, algebra]

1.3 For $0<x\le\rho<1$, the chain rule and [F4] show that $d\log(1-x)/dx=-1/(1-x)=-1-x/(1-x)$. Integrating from $0$ to $x$, using $\log(1)=0$, gives $\log(1-x)=-x-\int_0^x\frac{t}{1-t}\,dt,\qquad 0\le\int_0^x\frac{t}{1-t}\,dt\le\frac{1}{1-\rho}\int_0^x t\,dt=\frac{x^2}{2(1-\rho)}.$ For $t\in[0, x]$, $0\le t/(1-t)\le t/(1-\rho)$. Thus [F5] and $\int_0^x t\,dt=x^2/2$ give the displayed bound. By [F2], $\log(\omega_R/\omega_E)=\frac12[\log(1-x_E)-\log(1-x_R)]$. Inserting the integral identity separates the linear term $(x_R-x_E)/2=s(1/r_R-1/r_E)/2$. The remaining terms have absolute value at most half the sum of their nonnegative integral bounds, namely $(x_E^2+x_R^2)/(4(1-\rho))$. [F2, F4, F5, given, algebra, algebra]

2.1 The exact ratios, acceleration magnitude and uniform remainder bound are all consequences of the stated model identities; no empirical input is used. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, A1] ∎
## Remarks

- The static congruence is accelerated. The divergence of its required proper acceleration as $r\downarrow s$ is not a divergence of the Schwarzschild curvature invariant and does not make the exterior-coordinate boundary a curvature singularity.
- The frequency ratio assumes an ideal geometric-optics ray. Propagation through matter, finite wavelength, moving endpoints and measurement apparatus require additional models.

## Example

Let $s>0$ and compare static emitter and receiver radii $r_E=2s$, $r_R=4s$ over the same Schwarzschild exterior model. Here $f(2s)=1/2$ and $f(4s)=3/4$.

1. The exact model ratios are

   $$\frac{\omega_R}{\omega_E}=\sqrt{\frac{f(2s)}{f(4s)}}=\sqrt{\frac23},\qquad \frac{\Delta\tau_R}{\Delta\tau_E}=\sqrt{\frac{f(4s)}{f(2s)}}=\sqrt{\frac32}.$$

   The static proper acceleration at $2s$ is $a(2s)=c^2/(4\sqrt2s)$.
2. Write $r=s(1+\epsilon)$ for $\epsilon>0$. The exact static proper acceleration is

   $$a(r)=\frac{c^2}{2s\sqrt\epsilon(1+\epsilon)^{3/2}},$$

   which tends to $+\infty$ as $\epsilon\downarrow0$. In contrast, the curvature scalar has limit $K\to12/s^4$ by [[lem-gr-schwarzschild-curvature-and-kretschmann-scalar]], and the advanced extension chart is smooth through $r=s$ by [[lem-gr-schwarzschild-extension-chart]]. The acceleration divergence is therefore a property of maintaining a static worldline near the boundary, not evidence of a curvature blow-up there.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Schwarzschild exterior with $s>0$, static observers at $2s$ and $4s$, and an ideal ray in the geometric-optics reading.

[F1] For static observers, $\Delta\tau=\sqrt f\,\Delta t$, the observer-energy ratio is $\omega_R/\omega_E=\sqrt{f_E/f_R}$, and proper acceleration is $c^2s/(2r^2\sqrt f)$ ([[pthm-rpm-static-clock-redshift]]).

[F2] The curvature scalar is $K=12s^2/r^6$ in the Schwarzschild exterior and has boundary limit $12/s^4$ as $r\downarrow s$ ([[lem-gr-schwarzschild-curvature-and-kretschmann-scalar]]).

[F3] The advanced extension chart is a smooth Lorentzian extension through $r=s$, isometric to the exterior on $r>s$ ([[lem-gr-schwarzschild-extension-chart]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** substitute the two radii into the exact static formulas, then evaluate the proper-acceleration and curvature limits separately.


1.1 Substitution gives $f_E=1/2$ and $f_R=3/4$. Applying [F1] yields the frequency and clock ratios. The acceleration at $2s$ is $c^2s/[2(2s)^2\sqrt{1/2}]=c^2/(4\sqrt2s)$. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 At $r=s(1+\epsilon)$, $f=\epsilon/(1+\epsilon)$, so [F1] gives $a=c^2/[2s\sqrt\epsilon(1+\epsilon)^{3/2}]$, which diverges as $\epsilon\downarrow0$. By [F2], $K=12s^2/[s^6(1+\epsilon)^6]$ tends to $12/s^4$, a finite value. [F1, F2, algebra, algebra]

2.1 [F3] supplies a smooth extension through the same $r=s$ boundary. Hence the divergence in 1.2 is the static-observer acceleration requirement in the exterior chart, while this curvature scalar remains finite and the metric has the stated smooth extension. No measured clock ratio or acceleration is asserted. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F2, F3, given] ∎

## Postulate

Assume Countable Choice as inherited from [[def-rpm-body-moments]]. For a neutral test body, let $z:I\to M$ be a $C^2$ future timelike curve parametrized by proper time, let $U=dz/d\tau$, and let $p^a$ and $S^{ab}=-S^{ba}$ be the momentum and spin moments of [[def-rpm-body-moments]]. Adopt the pole-dipole evolution equations
$$D_\tau p^a=-\frac12 R^a{}_{bcd}U^bS^{cd},\qquad D_\tau S^{ab}=p^aU^b-p^bU^a.$$
A spin-supplementary condition (SSC) is an additional equation $S^{ab}n_b=0$ for a specified future unit timelike field $n$ along $z$; this postulate does not select one SSC, and $p$ is an independently evolved moment rather than a primitive assumption $p=mU$.

For a retained quadrupole or higher-multipole model, adopt
$$D_\tau p^a=-\frac12 R^a{}_{bcd}U^bS^{cd}+f_{\rm extra}^a,\qquad D_\tau S^{ab}=p^aU^b-p^bU^a+N_{\rm extra}^{ab},$$
where $f_{\rm extra}$ is a specified smooth force map along the state and $N_{\rm extra}^{ab}=-N_{\rm extra}^{ba}$ is a specified smooth torque map. A quadrupole convention that may be adopted is
$$f_{\rm quad}^a=-\frac16J^{bcde}\nabla^aR_{bcde},\qquad N_{\rm quad}^{ab}=\frac43R^{[a}{}_{cde}J^{b]cde},$$
with $J^{bcde}$ satisfying the algebraic symmetries of the curvature tensor, carrying units $\mathrm{kg\,m^4\,s^{-2}}$, and brackets including the factor $1/2$. Any evolved $J$ or higher moment needs its own transport or constitutive law; without it the multipole equations are not a closed initial-value model.

The pole-dipole and multipole equations are adopted finite-dimensional truncations, not derivations from the moment integrals above. Their use as approximations for a material body is restricted to regimes in which its size is small compared with the relevant curvature and background-variation lengths and omitted moment effects are negligible on the stated finite interval. These conditions are qualitative applicability assumptions here: this postulate supplies no uniform error bound, no convergence of truncations, and no global existence claim. No experimental result or measurement is asserted.

## Physical scope

The pole-dipole clause is neutral and test-body only. The optional multipole clause applies only when every extra force, torque, and evolved moment has explicit smooth constitutive data. No electric or magnetic dipole force is included in the BMT translation model, and no radiation reaction, self-force, singular-field evaluation, or quantum-spin claim is included.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice as inherited by the supplied Lorentzian smooth-structure and connection results. Let $z:I\to M$ be a $C^2$ future timelike worldline in a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,N)$, parametrized by proper time, with $U=D_\tau z$ and $g(U,U)=-c^2$. Let $p$ be a $C^1$ vector field along $z$, let $S^{ab}=-S^{ba}$ and $\mathcal T^{ab}=-\mathcal T^{ba}$ be $C^1$ bivector fields along $z$, and let $n$ be a $C^1$ future unit timelike field along $z$. Suppose
$$S^{ab}n_b=0,\qquad D_\tau S^{ab}=p^aU^b-p^bU^a+\mathcal T^{ab}.$$
Define $\gamma:=-g(n,U)/c$ and $E_n:=-c\,g(p,n)$. Then $\gamma>0$, and
$$c\gamma\,p^a=\frac{E_n}{c}U^a+S^{ab}D_\tau n_b+\mathcal T^{ab}n_b.$$
Here $\mathcal T$ denotes an arbitrary antisymmetric torque; setting it to zero gives the torque-free case.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Lorentzian manifold, its metric-compatible connection, the stated future timelike proper-time worldline, vector and bivector fields along it, a future unit field $n$, the SSC and the spin evolution equation.

[A1] Countable Choice is inherited through the supplied GR smooth-structure and connection items. [[def-countable-choice]]

[A2] Along the same proper-time curve, the observer satisfies $S^{ab}n_b=0$ and the antisymmetric fields obey $D_\tau S^{ab}=p^aU^b-p^bU^a+\mathcal T^{ab}$, with the stated regularity.

[F1] Proper-time parametrization of a future timelike Lorentzian worldline gives $g(U,U)=-c^2$. [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]

[F2] The covariant derivative along a curve satisfies the product rule on a pairing, and metric compatibility gives $D_\tau g=0$. [[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]; [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]

[F3] For a future unit timelike observer $n$ and future timelike $U/c$, $-g(n,U/c)>0$. [[lem-gr-observer-pairing-with-future-causal-vectors]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Differentiate the SSC in [A2] along $z$ using the inherited smooth-structure assumption and covariant product rule, then substitute its spin evolution equation:
$$0=D_\tau(S^{ab}n_b)=p^a g(U,n)-U^a g(p,n)+\mathcal T^{ab}n_b+S^{ab}D_\tau n_b.$$
Every term is defined at the same point of $z$, so the covariant product rule applies without comparing different tangent fibres. [given, A1, A2, F2, algebra]

2.1 The definitions give $g(U,n)=-c\gamma$ and $g(p,n)=-E_n/c$. Substitution into step 1.1 and rearrangement yield
$$c\gamma\,p^a=\frac{E_n}{c}U^a+\mathcal T^{ab}n_b+S^{ab}D_\tau n_b.$$
Positivity of $\gamma$ follows from [F3]. [given, A2, step 1.1, F1, F3, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

This is tensor algebra along one specified curve. It does not select an SSC, prove closure of the MPD equations, or identify $p$ with $mU$.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and use a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,N)$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ with its metric-compatible Levi–Civita connection. Use SI units: coordinates are metres, proper time is seconds, $c>0$ is in metres per second, $p$ is in kilogram metres per second, $S$ is in kilogram metres squared per second, and $R$ has inverse-square-metre components. Let $z:I\to M$ be a $C^2$ future timelike worldline parametrized by proper time, with $U=dz/d\tau$ and $g(U,U)=-c^2$. Let $p$ be a $C^1$ future timelike vector field along $z$, let $S^{ab}=-S^{ba}$ be a $C^1$ bivector field, and suppose the displayed evolution equations hold:

$$D_\tau p^a=f^a:=-\frac12R^a{}_{bcd}U^bS^{cd},\qquad D_\tau S^{ab}=p^aU^b-p^bU^a.\tag{1}$$

Put $\mu:=\sqrt{-g(p,p)}>0$, $m:=-g(p,U)/c^2>0$, $C^a:=S^{ab}p_b$, and define the linear map

$$K^a{}_b:=\mu^2\delta^a_b-\frac12S^{ac}R_{cbde}S^{de}.$$

At every state where $K$ is invertible and $W:=K^{-1}p$ is future timelike, the TD condition $C=0$ and (1) imply

$$KU=mc^2p,\qquad U=\frac{cW}{\sqrt{-g(W,W)}}.\tag{2}$$

## Statement

Let $S$ have $N\ge2$ states, positive detailed-balance law $\pi$, and connected undirected rate graph as in [[def-td-detailed-balance-rate-model]]. For every strictly positive initial probability vector $p(0)$, the master equation has a unique strictly positive probability solution $p(t)$ for all $t\ge0$. The relative entropy $D(p(t)\Vert\pi)=\sum_i p_i(t)\log(p_i(t)/\pi_i)$ is nonincreasing, and $p_i(t)\to\pi_i$ for every state. No monotonicity of Shannon entropy $-\sum_i p_i\log p_i$ is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite state set of size $N\ge2$, finite rates, a positive normalized detailed-balance vector $\pi$, and an initially strictly positive normalized vector $p(0)$.

[F1] [[def-td-detailed-balance-rate-model]]: $q_{ij}\ge0$ for $i\ne j$, $q_{ii}=-\sum_{j\ne i}q_{ij}$, and $\dot p_i=\sum_{j\ne i}(p_jq_{ji}-p_iq_{ij})$.

[F2] [[def-td-detailed-balance-rate-model]]: $a_{ij}:=\pi_iq_{ij}=\pi_jq_{ji}$ is positive on graph edges, and the graph is connected.

[F3] [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: $\log(xy)=\log x+\log y$, $\log(1/x)=-\log x$, and $\log x\le0$ for $0<x\le1$.

[F4] [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]], [[thm-chain-rule]], and [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: for $x>0$, $(\log x)'=1/x$, and the ordinary chain and finite-product rules differentiate the entropy sum.

[F5] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]] and [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: differentiate $e^{ct}$ and infer monotonicity on an interval from a nonpositive derivative.

[F6] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: the finite Cauchy--Schwarz inequality bounds a sum of at most $N-1$ edge increments by $(N-1)$ times their squared sum.

## Proof

**Given:** [F1]--[F6] and $p_i(0)>0$.

1.1 Put $c=1+\max_i\sum_{j\ne i}q_{ij}$ and $P=I+Q/c$, where $Q=(q_{ij})$. Then $P$ has nonnegative entries and row sums one. The series $p(t)=e^{-ct}\sum_{n=0}^\infty (ct)^n p(0)P^n/n!$ and its differentiated series converge uniformly on bounded time intervals; its coefficients are nonnegative and sum to one, so it is a probability vector, starts at $p(0)$, and differentiates to $\dot p=pQ$. Its $n=0$ term gives $p_i(t)\ge e^{-ct}p_i(0)>0$. For uniqueness, the difference $z$ of two solutions satisfies $z'=zQ$; with $C=\max_i\sum_j|q_{ij}|$ and $U(t)=\int_0^t\|z(s)\|_1ds$, one has $U'(t)=\|z(t)\|_1\le C U(t)$. Thus $(e^{-Ct}U(t))'\le0$ and $U(0)=0\le U(t)$ force $U=0$, hence $z=0$. [F1, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 With $r_i=p_i/\pi_i$, detailed balance gives $\dot p_i=\sum_{j\ne i}a_{ij}(r_j-r_i)$. By [F4], differentiating the finite entropy sum gives $D'=\sum_i\dot p_i(\log r_i+1)=\sum_i\dot p_i\log r_i$, since $\sum_i\dot p_i=0$. Pairing the $i,j$ terms gives $D'=-\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}a_{ij}(r_i-r_j)(\log r_i-\log r_j)\le0$: if $r_i\ge r_j$, then $\log r_i-\log r_j=-\log(r_j/r_i)\ge0$ by [F3], and the reversed order gives the same product sign. The mean value theorem [F5] on each compact time interval makes $D$ nonincreasing. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1]

2.2 Set $u_i=r_i-1$, so $\sum_i\pi_i u_i=0$, and $V(t)=\sum_i\pi_i u_i^2$. Since $\dot u_i=\pi_i^{-1}\sum_{j\ne i}a_{ij}(u_j-u_i)$, differentiating and pairing the two orientations of each edge gives $V'=2\sum_i u_i\sum_{j\ne i}a_{ij}(u_j-u_i)=-2\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}a_{ij}(u_i-u_j)^2$. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Let $a_*=\min_{\{i,j\}\in E}a_{ij}>0$. Fix a root state and choose one simple path from it to each state; this is only a finite family of choices, obtainable successively, and each path has length at most $N-1$. Telescoping and [F6] give $(u_i-u_r)^2\le(N-1)\sum_{\{j,k\}\in E}(u_j-u_k)^2$. The zero-mean identity gives $u_r=-\sum_i\pi_i(u_i-u_r)$; expanding $\sum_i\pi_i[(u_i-u_r)-\sum_j\pi_j(u_j-u_r)]^2\ge0$ yields $u_r^2\le\sum_i\pi_i(u_i-u_r)^2$. Since $(x+y)^2\le2x^2+2y^2$ and $\sum_i\pi_i=1$, it follows that $V\le4(N-1)\sum_E(u_i-u_j)^2\le4(N-1)a_*^{-1}\sum_Ea_{ij}(u_i-u_j)^2$. [F2, F6, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Thus $V'\le-2\lambda V$ with $\lambda=a_*/[4(N-1)]>0$. By [F5], the derivative of $e^{2\lambda t}V(t)$ is nonpositive and that function is nonincreasing, so $V(t)\le e^{-2\lambda t}V(0)$. Since $\pi_i u_i(t)^2\le V(t)$ and $p_i-\pi_i=\pi_i u_i$, each $p_i(t)\to\pi_i$. [F5, step 2.2, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

For $t>0$ define
$$T(x,t)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Gamma(x-y,at)g(y)\,dy,\qquad \Gamma(z,\theta)=(4\pi\theta)^{-3/2}e^{-|z|^2/(4\theta)},$$
and set $T(x,0)=g(x)$ on $\overline\Omega$. This field is the unique $C^1$-in-time, $C^2$-in-space solution on each finite time interval of $c\partial_tT=k\Delta T$ on $\Omega$, with $\partial_nT=0$ on every face and the given initial value. It satisfies $T_{\min}\le T(x,t)\le T_{\max}$ for all $t\ge0$, has $C^2$ spatial derivatives continuous to $t=0$, and its right time derivative there is $a\Delta g$. Under [[post-td-local-energy-balance]] and [[post-td-fourier-conductivity]], it is a global-in-time solution of that restricted physical continuum model.

**Given:** Countable Choice; a three-dimensional rectangle with positive side lengths; constants $c,k>0$; and an even, $2L_i$-periodic $C^2$ function $g$ with bounded uniformly continuous derivatives and $0<T_{\min}\le g\le T_{\max}$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: for every sequence of nonempty sets there is a function selecting one element from each set. Countable Choice is the only choice principle assumed here.

[A2] The material has constant volumetric heat capacity $u'(T)=c>0$ on the whole range $[T_{\min},T_{\max}]$; this is an explicit caloric restriction, not a consequence of the heat equation.

[A3] [[post-td-local-energy-balance]]: $\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}j_Q=0$ and $j_Q\cdot n=0$ on each insulated face.

[A4] [[post-td-fourier-conductivity]]: $j_Q=-K\nabla T$; the constant scalar case is $K=kI_3$.

[F1] [[thm-heat-cauchy-solution-for-bounded-continuous-data]]: assuming Countable Choice, convolution of a bounded uniformly continuous $g:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ with the Gaussian heat kernel gives a bounded function, smooth for positive time, solving $U_\theta=\Delta U$, and converging locally uniformly to $g$ as $\theta\downarrow0$.

[F2] [[lem-heat-kernel-normalisation-scaling-and-derivatives]]: $\Gamma(z,\theta)>0$, has unit integral, and its derivatives have Gaussian tail bounds; $\Gamma(\cdot,\theta)$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity as $\theta\downarrow0$.

[F3] [[lem-spatial-and-time-derivatives-pass-through-heat-convolution-for-positive-time]]: for bounded data the heat convolution is smooth for positive time, derivatives pass through its integral, and $U_\theta=\Delta U$.

[F4] [[cor-l-one-approximate-identities-converge-uniformly-on-compacta-for-continuous-functions]]: convolution by an $L^1$ approximate identity converges uniformly on every compact set for bounded continuous data.

[F5] [[def-td-rectangular-local-equilibrium-fields]]: $T,u,c,j_Q,K$ have the domains, regularity classes, Euclidean derivatives, and SI units stated in its Definition.

[F6] [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]: translation preserves Lebesgue measure.

[F7] [[thm-linear-change-of-variables-for-lebesgue-measure]]: under Countable Choice, an invertible linear map changes Lebesgue measure by the absolute determinant of its matrix.

[F8] [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]: a continuous function on a closed interval with an integrable interior derivative has endpoint increment equal to the derivative integral.

[F9] [[def-heat-kernel]]: for $\theta>0$, $\Gamma(z,\theta)=(4\pi\theta)^{-3/2}\exp(-|z|^2/(4\theta))$ on $\mathbb R^3$.

[F10] [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: absolutely integrable functions on sigma-finite product measure spaces have equal iterated and product integrals.

## Postulate

Here $Z$ is dimensionless, positive, and finite because $\Omega$ is finite and nonempty.

The same adopted law may be assigned to a specified countable state model with its stated enumeration and energy list, or to a measurable model $(X,\Sigma,\mu,E)$ with a dimensionless reference measure $\mu$ and measurable energy $E:X\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$, only when $0<Z(\beta)<\infty$ for the declared series or integral. In those cases $P_\beta(i)=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$ or the probability density is $p_\beta=e^{-\beta E}/Z$ relative to $\mu$. The countable and integral conventions are those of [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]] and [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]] at their actual current draft statements.

This is an adopted statistical-mechanical preparation rule. It is not derived from the macroscopic thermodynamic laws, a finite bath, entropy maximization, or a time-evolution equation. It does not assert that a physical sample has this preparation; that identification is an additional model assumption to be tested against a specified preparation and apparatus.

## Statement

Let $(\Omega,\epsilon)$ be a finite microstate model with energies $E_x=\epsilon(x)\,\mathrm J$ from [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]]. Let $T>0$, $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$, and $P_\beta(x)=e^{-\beta E_x}/Z(\beta)$ be the adopted preparation of [[post-td-canonical-sampling]]. With $\bar E_\beta=\sum_xP_\beta(x)E_x$, $\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)=\sum_xP_\beta(x)(E_x-\bar E_\beta)^2$, and $S_\beta=-k_{\mathrm B}\sum_xP_\beta(x)\log P_\beta(x)$, the finite partition sum is positive and
$$-\partial_\beta\log Z=\bar E_\beta,\qquad \partial_\beta^2\log Z=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E),\qquad S_\beta=k_{\mathrm B}(\log Z+\beta\bar E_\beta).$$
Consequently the statistical free-energy value $F_{\mathrm{stat}}:=-k_{\mathrm B}T\log Z$ satisfies $F_{\mathrm{stat}}=\bar E_\beta-TS_\beta$. The derivatives hold the finite state set and its energy list fixed. No equivalence with a macroscopic entropy or Helmholtz potential is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite nonempty state set, a fixed energy list in joules, $T>0$, the fixed SI value of $k_{\mathrm B}$, and the adopted canonical weights.

[F1] [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]]: $\Omega$ is finite and nonempty and each $E_x$ is a fixed energy in joules.

[F2] [[post-td-canonical-sampling]]: $P_\beta(x)=e^{-\beta E_x}/Z$ with $Z=\sum_xe^{-\beta E_x}$ and $\beta=1/(k_{\mathrm B}T)>0$ in $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$.

[F3] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]: $\frac{d}{d\beta}e^{-\beta E_x}=-E_xe^{-\beta E_x}$ for each fixed $E_x$.

[F4] [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]] and [[def-natural-logarithm]]: for differentiable positive $Z$, $(\log Z)'=Z'/Z$.

## Proof

**Given:** The finite canonical model and its fixed energy values.

1.1 Since $\Omega$ is finite and nonempty and every $e^{-\beta E_x}>0$, the finite sum $Z=\sum_xe^{-\beta E_x}$ is strictly positive and finite. The weights $P_\beta(x)$ therefore sum to one by their definition. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Differentiating the finite sum term by term using [F3] gives $Z'=-\sum_xE_xe^{-\beta E_x}$ and $Z''=\sum_xE_x^2e^{-\beta E_x}$. Applying [F4] yields $-\partial_\beta\log Z=-(Z'/Z)=\bar E_\beta$ and $\partial_\beta^2\log Z=Z''/Z-(Z'/Z)^2=\sum_xP_\beta(x)E_x^2-\bar E_\beta^2=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)$. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 For each $x$, $\log P_\beta(x)=-\beta E_x-\log Z$. Substituting this into the finite entropy sum gives $S_\beta=-k_{\mathrm B}\sum_xP_\beta(x)\log P_\beta(x)=k_{\mathrm B}(\beta\bar E_\beta+\log Z)$. Since $\beta k_{\mathrm B}=1/T$, rearrangement gives $\bar E_\beta-TS_\beta=-k_{\mathrm B}T\log Z=F_{\mathrm{stat}}$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let two finite microstate models from [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]] have nonempty state sets $\Omega_A,\Omega_B$, energies $E_A,E_B$ in joules, and the same $T>0$. Under the canonical sampling assumption [[post-td-canonical-sampling]], the partition function factorizes as $Z_{AB}=Z_AZ_B$, the joint canonical law is $P_{AB}=P_AP_B$, the Gibbs entropy satisfies $S_{AB}=S_A+S_B$, and the statistical free-energy value satisfies $F_{AB}=F_A+F_B$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Two finite nonempty state sets, additive composite energy, fixed $T>0$, and the canonical preparations of both subsystems and their composite.

2.1 Since each probability is positive, $\log P_{AB}(x,y)=\log P_A(x)+\log P_B(y)$. Summing against $P_A(x)P_B(y)$ and using the finite normalizations yields $S_{AB}=S_A+S_B$. The mean energy is $\bar E_{AB}=\bar E_A+\bar E_B$ by the same finite factorization, so $F_{AB}=\bar E_{AB}-TS_{AB}=F_A+F_B$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For the forward path law of [[def-td-driven-finite-path-model]], under [[post-td-canonical-protocol-preparation]] and [[post-td-stationary-bath-kernel]], the finite expectation satisfies $\mathbb E_F[e^{-\beta W}]=Z_m/Z_0=e^{-\beta\Delta F}$. **Given:** A nonempty finite state space, finite energies $E_k$, $\beta>0$, a row-stochastic $K_k$, initial law $\pi_0$, and $\pi_kK_k=\pi_k$ at each stage.

**Proof technique:** induction on protocol stages.

2.1 For the induction step fix $k\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and suppose $S_{k-1}(i)=(Z_{k-1}/Z_0)\pi_{k-1}(i)$ for every $i$. [ih, step 1.1, F1]

3.1 Substitute this hypothesis in the recurrence from step 1.1. ## Remark

**Scope and objects.**

For a declared continuum model, let $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be an open spatial region with coordinates in metres and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval with coordinates in seconds. The model chooses a local-state parameter set $\mathcal Z\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ and a field $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_m)$ whose component functions have continuous first partial derivatives in the spatial coordinates and time on $\mathcal O\times I$. A component temperature field has type $T:\mathcal O\times I\to(0,\infty)$ and values in kelvins. If the model includes mass density and fluid velocity, their types are $\rho:\mathcal O\times I\to[0,\infty)$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ and $\mathbf u:\mathcal O\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; these fields may also be required to have continuous first partial derivatives. Each model must specify its remaining coordinates and equation of state; $\mathcal Z$ is not universal.

A **local-equilibrium approximation** is the model assumption that each coarse-grained cell at $(\mathbf x,t)$ is represented by the equilibrium constitutive state labelled by $z(\mathbf x,t)$. A mean free path $\ell>0\,\mathrm m$ is the model's typical distance between scattering events; a field-variation length $L>0\,\mathrm m$ is the smallest declared spatial scale over which $z$ changes appreciably. A collision time $\tau_{\mathrm c}>0\,\mathrm s$ is a declared microscopic relaxation time, and a protocol time $\tau_{\mathrm m}>0\,\mathrm s$ is the timescale of imposed variation. A kinetic local-equilibrium regime may require $\ell/L\ll1$ and $\tau_{\mathrm c}/\tau_{\mathrm m}\ll1$. These are qualitative regime inequalities, not universal numerical thresholds. In kinetic descriptions the actual distribution may be $f=f_0(z)+\delta f$; the local-equilibrium distribution alone need not solve the evolution equation.

Nonconstant fields $T(\mathbf x,t)$, $\rho(\mathbf x,t)$, or $\mathbf u(\mathbf x,t)$ are permitted in this continuum model and do not describe global equilibrium. ## Remark

**Scope.**

The adopted [[post-td-macroscopic-second-law]] compares the total macroscopic entropies of specified equilibrium endpoints of an admitted isolated process record. It assigns no entropy function to nonequilibrium intermediate configurations and does not assert that every microscopic realization has nonnegative entropy change. The macrostate and finite-model quantities remain distinct as defined in [[def-td-macro-versus-micro-entropy-claim]].

A stochastic fluctuation claim needs its own state space or path space, probability law, preparation, driving protocol, time interval, measured or modelled random variable, and averaging convention. A duration $\tau>0$ is in seconds; a trajectory observable has the units stated by its model (for physical entropy production, $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$; for dimensionless entropy production, no units). If a trajectory variable is called entropy production, define it and state the hypotheses of the relation being used, including the forward and reverse protocols and the support and integrability conditions needed for the stated averages. Positivity of an ensemble mean does not imply positivity in every realization.

For a precise model, let $X$ be its state space and $\Gamma$ its specified set of sample paths $\gamma:[0,\tau]\to X$, for a fixed duration $\tau>0$. An adopted probability measure $P$ on $\Gamma$ makes an observable $\Sigma:\Gamma\to\mathbb R$ a random variable; its mean $\mathbb E_P[\Sigma]$ is used only when $\Sigma$ is $P$-integrable. A driving protocol is a declared control map $\lambda:[0,\tau]\to\Lambda$, with its parameter space $\Lambda$, regularity and endpoint controls specified by the model. Any reverse-protocol comparison needs its own path measure and support conditions.

The fluctuation–dissipation theorem discussed in the cited treatments relates equilibrium fluctuations to a specified linear response of a coupled model. It is distinct from a trajectory fluctuation relation and does not by itself prove the macroscopic second-law postulate. No universal microscopic fluctuation formula or trajectory-wise entropy inequality is asserted here.

## Postulate

For the harmonic potential $U(x)=kx^2/2$ with position $x$ in metres, stiffness $k>0$ in joules per square metre, constant mobility $\mu>0$ in square metres per joule-second, and a bath at fixed $T_b>0$ kelvin, adopt the one-dimensional overdamped model $dX_t=-\gamma X_t\,dt+\sigma\,dB_t$, interpreted through the integral equation of [[def-tdmath-ornstein-uhlenbeck-equation]], with $\gamma=\mu k$ in seconds$^{-1}$ and $\sigma^2=2\mu k_{\mathrm B}T_b$ in square metres per second. Here $B$ is standard Brownian motion with its stated filtration and increment hypotheses, and the bath noise is independent of the initial preparation. This Einstein noise relation and the linear Markov model are physical assumptions. They do not follow from equilibrium thermodynamics alone and do not report a measured spectrum or calibration.

## Statement

Assume the filtered probability space, Brownian increment hypothesis, and initial data of [[def-tdmath-ornstein-uhlenbeck-equation]], including $\mathbb E X_0^2<\infty$ and future increments independent of $\mathcal F_0$. For $\gamma,\sigma>0$, on every finite time interval the process
$$X_t=e^{-\gamma t}X_0+\sigma e^{-\gamma t}\int_0^t e^{\gamma s}\,dB_s$$
has a continuous adapted version, solves the stated Ornstein–Uhlenbeck integral equation, and is the unique continuous solution driven by the same $(X_0,B)$. Put $V=\sigma^2/(2\gamma)$. For $0\le s<t$, its transition law conditional on $\mathcal F_s$ is normal with mean $e^{-\gamma(t-s)}X_s$ and variance $V(1-e^{-2\gamma(t-s)})$. Consequently
$$\mathbb E X_t=e^{-\gamma t}\mathbb E X_0,\qquad\operatorname{Var}(X_t)=e^{-2\gamma t}\operatorname{Var}(X_0)+V(1-e^{-2\gamma t}).$$
From any such initial law, $X_t$ converges in distribution to $N(0,V)$. If $X_0\sim N(0,V)$ and is independent of future Brownian increments, the process is stationary Gaussian with covariance $C(\tau)=Ve^{-\gamma|\tau|}$, and its transition kernel satisfies detailed balance with the $N(0,V)$ density. Its transition density solves the Fokker–Planck equation for positive time. Under the convention $S(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_{\mathbb R}C(\tau)e^{i\omega\tau}\,d\tau$, the stationary spectrum and time-average bound are
$$S(\omega)=\frac{V\gamma}{\pi(\gamma^2+\omega^2)},\qquad\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\frac1T\int_0^T X_t\,dt\right)\le\frac{2V}{\gamma T}.$$
All these statements concern the specified linear stochastic model. An Einstein relation between $\sigma$ and a physical bath temperature would be an additional physical postulate.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The exact Brownian filtration hypothesis and the OU equation definition.

[A1] $B$ is adapted and each increment $B_t-B_s$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ with law $N(0,t-s)$; $X_0$ is $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, has finite second moment, and is independent of future Brownian increments.

[A2] $\gamma>0$, $\sigma>0$, and time is restricted to an arbitrary finite interval $[0,T]$.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-ornstein-uhlenbeck-equation]]: a solution is a continuous adapted process satisfying $X_t=X_0-\gamma\int_0^tX_sds+\sigma B_t$ almost surely for every $t$.

[F2] [[def-brownian-motion]], [[thm-existence-of-continuous-brownian-motion]], and [[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]: Brownian paths have a common continuous version and deterministic continuous square-integrable integrands satisfy the standing predictable Brownian hypotheses on finite intervals.

[F3] [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] and [[thm-ito-isometry-and-linearity-in-predictable-l2]]: the stochastic integral is defined for the deterministic square-integrable integrand and isometry computes its second moments.

[F4] [[thm-ito-integral-process-has-a-continuous-martingale-version]] and [[cor-deterministic-ito-integrals-are-gaussian]]: the integral process has a continuous version, and deterministic-integrand integrals are centered Gaussian with variance equal to the squared-integrand integral.

[F5] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]] and [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: the ordinary exponential derivative and finite continuous-integral Fubini identity hold.

[F6] [[def-complex-exponential]] and [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]]: complex exponential phases are continuous, have unit modulus on the imaginary axis, and integrate by their elementary antiderivative.

[F7] [[thm-gaussian-integral]]: the centered Gaussian density with variance $v>0$ is normalized after the linear change of variable from the unit Gaussian.

## Proof



**Given:** [A1]–[A2] and [F1]–[F7].

1.1 On $[0,T]$, $g(s)=e^{\gamma s}$ is deterministic, continuous, and square-integrable. Thus $W_t=\int_0^t g(s)\,dB_s$ is defined by [F3], and [F4] supplies a continuous version. For a partition $0=t_0<\cdots<t_n=t$, the deterministic step sums $\sum_k g(t_k)(B_{t_{k+1}}-B_{t_k})$ converge in $L^2$ to $W_t$ by the Itô isometry and uniform approximation of $g$. Discrete summation by parts rewrites them as $g(t)B_t-g(0)B_0-\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}B_{t_{k+1}}(g(t_{k+1})-g(t_k))$ up to an endpoint term tending to zero. Brownian path continuity makes the last sums converge pathwise to $\int_0^t g'(s)B_sds$. The $L^2$ limit and this almost-sure limit agree in probability, so $$W_t=e^{\gamma t}B_t-\gamma\int_0^t e^{\gamma s}B_s\,ds$$ almost surely for each fixed $t$. Both sides have continuous versions; equality on rational $t$ holds on one probability-one event and therefore extends to all $t\in[0,T]$. [A1, A2, F2, F3, F4, F5]

1.2 Split the stochastic integral at $s$ and use its linearity: $$X_t=e^{-\gamma(t-s)}X_s+\sigma\int_s^t e^{-\gamma(t-u)}\,dB_u.$$ Step-function approximants to the last deterministic-integrand integral depend only on increments after $s$, so [A1] makes them independent of $\mathcal F_s$. Their $L^2$ limit remains independent of $\mathcal F_s$: for bounded $\mathcal F_s$-measurable $Y$ and bounded continuous $\varphi$, convergence in probability plus boundedness gives convergence of $\mathbb E[Y\varphi(\cdot)]$, preserving the factorization. By [F4] the limit is centered Gaussian; [F3] computes its variance as $\sigma^2\int_s^t e^{-2\gamma(t-u)}du=V(1-e^{-2\gamma(t-s)})$. This proves the conditional transition law and the Markov property. [A1, A2, F3, F4]

2.1 Set $X_t=e^{-\gamma t}X_0+\sigma e^{-\gamma t}W_t$. By [F4] it is continuous and adapted. Step 1.1 rewrites it as $$X_t=e^{-\gamma t}X_0+\sigma B_t-\sigma\gamma\int_0^t e^{-\gamma(t-s)}B_s\,ds.$$ Integrating this continuous expression in $t$, ordinary Fubini [F5] gives $$\int_0^tX_sds=X_0(1-e^{-\gamma t})/\gamma+\sigma\int_0^tB_sds-\sigma\int_0^tB_u(1-e^{-\gamma(t-u)})\,du.$$ Substitution into $X_0-\gamma\int_0^tX_sds+\sigma B_t$ cancels the two $\int B_sds$ terms and leaves exactly the displayed expression for $X_t$. Thus [F1] holds. [A1, A2, F1, F4, F5, step 1.1]

2.2 Taking expectations in the explicit solution, the stochastic integral has mean zero by [F4], giving $\mathbb E X_t=e^{-\gamma t}\mathbb E X_0$. The integral is independent of $X_0$ and centered, so its variance adds to $e^{-2\gamma t}\operatorname{Var}(X_0)$; [F3] evaluates the added variance as $V(1-e^{-2\gamma t})$. The independent Gaussian term tends in law to $N(0,V)$ because its variance tends to $V$ and $e^{-\gamma t}X_0\to0$ in $L^2$; for any bounded continuous test, restrict to a compact interval, use uniform continuity and the second-moment tail bound, then take the interval radius to infinity. [A1, A2, F3, F4, step 1.2]

2.3 Write $r=e^{-\gamma t}$ and $\pi(x)=(2\pi V)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/(2V)}$. The transition density is $$K_t(x,y)=[2\pi V(1-r^2)]^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(y-rx)^2}{2V(1-r^2)}\right).$$ Multiplying by $\pi(x)$ gives a symmetric prefactor and exponent proportional to $-[x^2+y^2-2rxy]/[2V(1-r^2)]$, unchanged when $x$ and $y$ are exchanged. Hence $\pi(x)K_t(x,y)=\pi(y)K_t(y,x)$, the detailed-balance identity. [A1, A2, F6, F7, step 1.2]

2.4 For $t>0$ let $\mu=e^{-\gamma t}x$, $v=V(1-e^{-2\gamma t})$, and $p(t,x,y)$ be the normal density with mean $\mu$ and variance $v$. Direct differentiation gives $$\partial_t p=p\left(\frac{\mu'(y-\mu)}v+\frac{v'}2\left[\frac{(y-\mu)^2}{v^2}-\frac1v\right]\right),\quad \mu'=-\gamma\mu,\quad v'=\sigma^2-2\gamma v.$$ Also direct $y$-differentiation gives $\gamma\partial_y(yp)+(\sigma^2/2)\partial_{yy}p$ equal to the same expression after writing $y=\mu+(y-\mu)$. Thus $\partial_t p=\gamma\partial_y(yp)+(\sigma^2/2)\partial_{yy}p$. The Gaussian formula has total integral one and converges to point mass at $x$ as $t\downarrow0$; this is the stated positive-time Fokker–Planck solution. [A2, F5, F7, step 1.2]

3.1 If $X$ and $\widetilde X$ are two continuous solutions with the same data, their difference $z$ satisfies $z(t)=-\gamma\int_0^tz(s)ds$. Let $D(t)=\int_0^t|z(s)|ds$. Then $D(0)=0$, $D\ge0$, and $D'(t)=|z(t)|\le\gamma D(t)$ by the equation. The derivative of $e^{-\gamma t}D(t)$ is nonpositive, so this nonnegative function is at most its initial value zero. Hence $D=0$ and continuity gives $z=0$ at every time. [A2, F1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 If $X_0$ is centered normal with variance $V$, step 1.2 gives centered Gaussian finite-dimensional laws, since each stochastic integral over a disjoint increment interval is an independent Gaussian and $X_0$ is independent of future increments. Its one-time variance is $V$. For $s\le t$, the split formula in 2.1 and independence of the later increment yield $\mathbb E[X_sX_t]=e^{-\gamma(t-s)}\mathbb E[X_s^2]=Ve^{-\gamma(t-s)}$. Thus covariance depends only on $|t-s|$. A centered Gaussian finite-dimensional law is determined by its covariance matrix; shifting every time by the same amount preserves that matrix and proves stationarity. [A1, A2, F4, step 1.2, step 2.2]

4.1 The stationary covariance is integrable. By evenness, $$S(\omega)=\frac V\pi\operatorname{Re}\int_0^\infty e^{-(\gamma-i\omega)t}dt =\frac V\pi\operatorname{Re}\frac1{\gamma-i\omega} =\frac{V\gamma}{\pi(\gamma^2+\omega^2)}.$$ The integral converges absolutely because $\gamma>0$. [A2, F6, step 3.2]

5.1 For the stationary time average, Fubini applies since $C$ is bounded on the finite square. Changing variables in the two triangular halves gives $$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(T^{-1}\int_0^TX_tdt\right) =\frac{2V}{T^2}\int_0^T(T-s)e^{-\gamma s}ds \le\frac{2V}{\gamma T}.$$ The bound tends to zero, so these averages converge to zero in $L^2$ and in probability. It asserts no almost-sure theorem for arbitrary observables. [A1, A2, F5, step 3.2] ∎
